title: Prevent Command History Logging
summary: Shells and other command interpreters keep a local record of what the operator typed, and an intruder who wants to hide their steps will often attack that record instead of the shell itself. On Linux and macOS the history is governed by environment variables: unsetting the variable that names the history file, setting the history file size to zero, or configuring history control to ignore entries that begin with a space each stop commands from being written to the history file when the session ends. On Windows, PowerShell records typed commands through the PSReadLine module into a file in the user profile, and either the save path or the save style can be changed so that nothing is written. Network devices with a command line interface can have their command logging switched off in the same way. The footprint is largely an absence, which is why defenders look at the remaining evidence: shell command lines that contain those variable assignments, process creation for the interpreter, changes to the size or timestamps of the history file, and a session whose history is far shorter than the activity around it suggests.

beginner.definition: This technique is about hiding the commands that an attacker types. Most shells save a list of the commands you enter. That list helps you retrace your work, and it helps investigators too. An attacker can change the settings so the list is never written.
beginner.whyItMatters: Command history is one of the cheapest records you have. If it is switched off, you lose the story of what happened on a host. The change itself is small and easy to miss, because it looks like a normal setting. Attackers may also put a space in front of each command to keep it out of the list. Collecting shell activity in a central place protects you from this.
howItWorks: On Linux and macOS, a shell keeps its history in a file named by an environment variable.
The attacker removes that variable, so the shell has nowhere to save its list.
They can also set the history size to zero, which stops the file from growing.
Another trick tells the shell to ignore commands that begin with a space.
On Windows, the PowerShell shell saves typed commands through a module called PSReadLine.
Its save path or save style can be changed, so the history file stays empty.
beginner.example: Picture a shop with a visitor book beside the door. Every guest writes their name and the time. The book helps the owner see who came and went. A thief does not steal the visitor book at all. They simply take the pen and hide it in a drawer. Guests still walk in and out all day. At closing time the owner finds a book with no new names. Missing command history is that missing pen, and the empty pages are your clue.
takeaways: Removing or shrinking command history is itself an event worth alerting on.
Send shell activity to a central log, so a local setting cannot hide it.
Compare a user's history file with their session activity to spot a gap.

objectives: Explain how Linux and macOS shells store command history and which settings control it.
Describe how PowerShell records typed commands through the PSReadLine module.
Identify the command lines that show history logging was weakened or disabled.
Explain how central logging compensates for a disabled local history file.
Describe how command logging on network devices can be switched off by an intruder.
